Provides the Critical Value(s) for a t-distribution

Source: R/cv_t.R
cv_t.Rd

Provides the Critical Value(s) for a t-distribution

Usage

cv_t(
  alpha_level,
  df,
  alternative = "not_equal",
  alpha_lower,
  alpha_upper,
  ncp = 0,
  verbose = TRUE
)

Arguments

alpha_level

Type I error rate (i.e., the false positive rate).

df

The number of degrees of freedom (a positive number)

alternative

The type of alternative hypothesis of interest.

alpha_lower

The error rate on the lower (negative) side of the distribution.

alpha_upper

The error rate on the upper (positive) side of the distribution.

ncp

The noncentral parameter (if zero, the default, it is the central t-distribution).

verbose

Provides extra information about areas under the curve.

Value

Returns the critical value(s), based on the input specifications, in a output style.

Details

Though a noncentral parameter can be included, that would not be done for a standard null hypothesis significance test.

With a nonzero ncp the critical values are quantiles of the noncentral t distribution, computed exactly. R's qt() and pt() with ncp switch to a normal approximation above a noncentrality of 37.62 (and above 33 with more than 2,000 degrees of freedom), where they can be far off: the .975 quantile with ncp = 50 and df = 3 is 186.49, and qt() gives 429.18. There the quantiles and the tail areas are computed by integrating over the sampling distribution of the standard deviation; inside that range they are R's. With fewer than one degree of freedom (df may be any positive number) pt() is not accurate inside that range either. At the exact quantiles of probability .0005 to .9995, with noncentralities up to 37.5 in absolute value, the tail probability it gave was off by as much as .14 with df = 0.05, .07 with 0.1, .01 with 0.2, .0013 with 0.3, \(3.8 \times 10^{-5}\) with 0.5, and \(2 \times 10^{-11}\) with 0.8, so with df < 1 every noncentral quantile and tail area is integrated. The critical values then differ from qt()'s by orders of magnitude with df of 0.3 or less (and by as much as 15 percent with 0.5): with df = 0.1, ncp = 0.5, and alpha_level = .05 they are \(-1.0428 \times 10^{10}\) and \(5.7095 \times 10^{13}\), where qt() gives -33554432 and 305284064. With so few degrees of freedom the tails are heavy enough that a critical value can lie beyond the largest number R represents (about \(1.8 \times 10^{308}\)); it is then returned as -Inf or Inf, as qt() returns it with ncp = 0 (with df = 0.001 one or both of the critical values are infinite at every alpha_level from .000001 to .4 and noncentrality from -100 to 100 tried).

References

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge.

See also

Other critical values: cv_bonferroni_f(), cv_bryant_paulson(), cv_chisq(), cv_dunnett(), cv_f(), cv_scheffe(), cv_smm(), cv_tukey_hsd(), cv_z()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# A basic call for finding critical values with equal area in the two tails.
cv_t(alpha_level = .05, df = 13)
#>  term     value  area_less area_greater
#>  lower_cv -2.160 0.025     0.975       
#>  upper_cv 2.160  0.975     0.025       

# A basic call for a single-sided confidence interval (for "a greater than" alternative hypothesis)
cv_t(alpha_level = .05, df = 13, alternative = "greater")
#>  term     value area_less area_greater
#>  lower_cv -Inf  0.000     1.000       
#>  upper_cv 1.771 0.950     0.050       

# A single-sided confidence interval (for "a greater than" alternative hypothesis); simple output.
cv_t(alpha_lower = 0, alpha_upper = .05, df = 13, verbose = FALSE)
#>  term     value
#>  lower_cv -Inf 
#>  upper_cv 1.771

# For a nonsymmetric 95% confidence interval.
cv_t(alpha_lower = .01, alpha_upper = .04, df = 13)
#>  term     value  area_less area_greater
#>  lower_cv -2.650 0.010     0.990       
#>  upper_cv 1.899  0.960     0.040
